item.title: Backing Up and Restoring SSH Keys
item.description:
When setting up a fresh system like my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 (named taylor) running Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition), transferring cryptographic identities safely is a top priority. When hardening SSH, the strictness of file permissions is enforced directly by OpenSSH's StrictModes check. If permissions are too open, SSH will reject key usage with errors like permissions being too open.

OpenSSH Permission Requirements

Here are the minimal and recommended permissions required for secure SSH key directory and file operations on your system.

The SSH Directory (~/.ssh)

  • Minimal/Recommended Permission: 700 (drwx------).
  • Access Level: Only the file owner can read, write, and execute the directory, leaving group and others with zero access.
  • Ownership: Must be owned by the active user account utilizing the keys.
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.ssh

Files Within the SSH Directory

Permissions vary depending on whether the file contains private data, public data, or configuration settings:

  • Private Keys (id_ed25519, id_rsa): Mode 600 (or 400) for owner read/write or read-only access, barring all others.
  • Public Keys (id_ed25519.pub, id_rsa.pub): Mode 644 allowing owner read/write and group/others read-only access.
  • Authorized Keys (authorized_keys): Mode 600 for owner read/write only.
  • Config / Known Hosts (config, known_hosts): Mode 600.

Note

For private key files, the absolute minimum required permission for standard SSH operations is 400 (-r--------). However, 600 is standard because it allows updating configurations without modifying permission bits first.

Parent Directory Constraints

OpenSSH also validates the permissions of parent directories in the path leading up to ~/.ssh. Your home directory must not be writable by group or world, with a maximum allowable mode of 755 or 750. If the home directory has overly open permissions, SSH will refuse key authentication even if ~/.ssh is set to 700.

chmod 750 /home/$USER

Backing Up and Restoring via External USB

To transfer your .ssh directory to an external USB drive from Fedora 44 and later restore it to taylor, standard copying tools can cause ownership mismatches or strip permission bits. Using rsync with the -p (--perms) flag ensures permission bits transfer intact while writing files directly under your current logged-in user.

Using rsync for Backup and Restoration

Assuming your USB directory mount path points to your target location, run the copy operation while preserving permissions:

rsync -rp /path/to/source/.ssh/ /path/to/destination/.ssh/

The flag breakdown includes:

  • `-r` (`--recursive`): Recurses into subdirectories and copies all files.
  • `-p` (`--perms`): Preserves explicit file permission modes.
  • No `-o`/`-g`: Running as a normal user without sudo automatically assigns your current $USER and primary group as the owner.

Alternative Using cp

If rsync is not available, you can perform the copy with cp:

cp -r --preserve=mode /path/to/source/.ssh /path/to/destination/.ssh

Post-Restore Verification and Hardening

After restoring your keys to taylor from the USB drive, perform a post-copy safety check and apply mass hardening commands to satisfy OpenSSH strict mode checks.

Inspection and Hardening Commands

Verify file permissions and apply the mass hardening script:

# 1. Inspect restored files
ls -la ~/.ssh

# 2. Set directory to 700 and private keys to 600
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_* 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/*.pub 2>/dev/null || true

# 3. Ensure proper user ownership
chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.ssh

Establishing Remote SSH Key Authentication

To connect from another machine—such as your MacBook Pro (running macOS)—to your Lenovo ThinkPad taylor (running Fedora 44) using SSH keys, you need to configure network access, verify the SSH daemon, and copy your public key.

Step 1: Find the IP Addresses

First, identify the local IP addresses of both systems.

On your Lenovo ThinkPad (Fedora Linux), open a terminal and run:

hostname -I

(Alternatively, use ``ip a`` and look for the ``inet`` address under your Wi-Fi or Ethernet interface).

On your MacBook Pro (macOS), open Terminal and run:

ipconfig getifaddr en0

(If connected via Wi-Fi, ``en0`` is typically your Wi-Fi interface).

Step 2: Ensure SSH Server is Running on Fedora

Before copying your key, ensure your ThinkPad allows incoming SSH connections. On your ThinkPad, run:

# Check if SSH daemon is active
systemctl status sshd

# If it is not active, start and enable it:
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd

# Ensure Fedora's firewall allows SSH traffic:
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

Step 3: Copy Your Key from MacBook Pro to ThinkPad

Because your key file may have a custom name (such as porfirio@altair.pub instead of the default id_ed25519.pub), you must pass the -i flag to specify it.

Run this command from your MacBook Pro Terminal (replace username with your Fedora username and 192.168.1.50 with your ThinkPad's IP):

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@altair.pub username@192.168.1.50
  1. Confirm the connection prompt by typing yes and hitting Enter.
  2. Enter your Fedora user password when prompted.
  3. The key will be installed into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on your ThinkPad.

Step 4: Configure ~/.ssh/config on Your MacBook Pro

Since your key file has a custom name, macOS will not automatically use it when running a standard SSH connection. To make connecting seamless, add an entry to your ~/.ssh/config file on your MacBook Pro:

  1. Open the configuration file on your Mac:

    nano ~/.ssh/config

  2. Add the following host block:

    Host taylor
    HostName 192.168.1.50
    User username
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/porfirio@altair

    (Replace ``192.168.1.50`` with your ThinkPad's IP and ``username`` with your Fedora account name).

  3. Save and exit (Ctrl + O, Enter, then Ctrl + X).

Step 5: Test Passwordless SSH

Now, from your MacBook Pro, you can connect passwordlessly by running:

ssh taylor

Finishing Touches

With these steps completed on Fedora 44, your SSH keys are safely backed up, restored, and fully optimized for secure remote connections.

item.title: Fedora Everything 44 Minimal Workstation
item.description:
A while ago at work, I was assigned a Lenovo ThinkPad T450. Recently, its original 128GB SSD running Debian Testing suffered a permanent hardware failure.

Hardware Failure and Data Recovery Strategy

The laptop's SSD began showing signs of wear before finally freezing mid-task while I was running Android Studio and an active collaborative project. Subsequent attempts to boot or reinstall an operating system failed completely, as the drive had locked itself into a permanent read-only state.

Fortunately, all development projects were properly mirrored in remote Git repositories, and critical local documents were preserved on secondary machines via incremental backups managed with rsync (a tool I will cover in a future publication).

Storage Upgrade and Hardware Maintenance

To restore the ThinkPad T450, I originally planned to acquire a 256GB Samsung 850 Pro. However, due to component price spikes driven by AI industry demand, I opted for a budget-friendly 240GB Crucial BX500 instead. On that same order, I also picked up a uni-ball Jetstream Prime Twist pen and a Kuru Toga Metal mechanical pencil (my first mechanical pencil in 17 years).

To my surprise, when the package arrived, the vendor had shipped a 480GB SanDisk SSD Plus instead of the 240GB drive—double the storage capacity for the same tier.

Received a 480GB SanDisk SSD Plus instead of the ordered 240GB drive.

I removed the bottom chassis cover of the T450, extracted the defective SSD, and mounted the new 480GB drive.

Taylor internals after removing a few screws and snapping off the bottom.

Then removed the old SSD from the enclosure.

Unboxed the new SSD.

My new SSD.

The new SSD is ready to be installed on Taylor.

After reassembling the chassis, I booted into the system BIOS to confirm that the new disk was properly recognized.

The new SSD is successfully recognized and listed on the boot menu.

Installation via Fedora Everything Netinstall

To maintain a lean, bloat-free system, I created installation media using the Fedora Everything Netinstall ISO (Release 44, x86_64) available from the official Fedora repository:

  • URL: https://fedoraproject.org/en/misc/#everything

Unlike the standard Live Workstation media, the Netinstall image allows explicit selection of individual package groups and components. Once options are finalized in the Anaconda installer, all necessary packages are fetched directly from the upstream Fedora mirrors. This ensures that every installed binary is completely up to date from minute one.

Taylor booting up from the installation media that contains the Fedora Everything Netinstall ISO for release 44, for x86_64 devices.

During the installation I made use of my Motorola ThinkPhone to share its Wi-Fi connection to Taylor via a Wired USB Tethering network:

This is a good example of how useful a USB Wired Network can be in some scenarios.

Once download and deployment completed, Anaconda performed a clean reboot into the fresh installation.

Installation completed and Taylor is ready to reboot.

This is Taylor's GRUB2 menu with the latest Linux kernel available for Fedora Linux 44 already installed:

Taylor booting up to Linux 7.2.7-200.

Upon selecting the kernel, I was prompted by the cryptsetup password manager to decrypt the disk:

Time to insert the passphrase.

This is Taylor's System Information under Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition) with GNOME Shell as Desktop Environment.

Minimal System Metrics and Metrics Overview

Below is a breakdown of metrics, repository lists, and package selections for this minimal Fedora 44 GNOME Shell Workstation setup:

Installation Date and Time

There are many ways to confirm when the Fedora installation started, when some filesystems or partitions were created, and when the installation process was completed with success.

One possible way is by inspecting the Anaconda Installer Logs. Fedora's installer, Anaconda, copies its logs over to the target system upon a successful installation. You can check the creation (birth) time of the primary installation log or kickstart configuration file:

stat /var/log/anaconda/anaconda.log

Which returns:

porfirio@taylor:~$ stat /var/log/anaconda/anaconda.log
  File: /var/log/anaconda/anaconda.log
  Size: 120716       Blocks: 240        IO Block: 4096   regular file
Device: 252,1        Inode: 262214      Links: 1
Access: (0600/-rw-------)  Uid: (    0/    root)   Gid: (    0/    root)
Context: system_u:object_r:var_log_t:s0
Access: 2026-10-11 03:57:53.378396125 +0000
Modify: 2026-09-27 07:01:52.682345253 +0000
Change: 2026-09-27 07:01:52.682345253 +0000
 Birth: 2026-09-27 07:01:52.681300526 +0000

Or:

sudo ls -l /root/anaconda-ks.cfg

Which returns:

porfirio@taylor:~$ sudo ls -l /root/anaconda-ks.cfg
[sudo] password for porfirio:
-rw-------. 1 root root 1207 Sep 27 07:01 /root/anaconda-ks.cfg

Another way is by checking the Root Filesystem Creation Date. Just like on Debian, the underlying filesystem's birth time can tell you when it was initialized:

Using stat on the root directory:

stat -c %w /

Which returns:

porfirio@taylor:~$ stat -c %w /
2026-09-27 06:47:23.000000000 +0000

It is also possible to use tune2fs (for ext4 filesystems):

sudo tune2fs -l $(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $1}') | grep 'Filesystem created:'

Which returned:

porfirio@taylor:~$sudo tune2fs -l$(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $1}') | grep 'Filesystem created:'
[sudo] password for porfirio:
Filesystem created:       Sun Sep 27 06:47:23 2026

Number of packages and amount of data downloaded

During the installation Anaconda downloaded 1905 packages, for a total of 2.02 GiB:

Anaconda getting the 1905 packages that would serve for a Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition).

After the installation got completed this was the total used space for the 1905 packages once installed:

Just 7.7 GB are required to have a fully functional Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition).

This is another way to see how the space is used on the disk by using the command line:

porfirio@taylor:~$ df -h
Filesystem                      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/fedora_taylor-root  428G  7.1G  399G   2% /
devtmpfs                        5.8G     0  5.8G   0% /dev
tmpfs                           5.8G   92K  5.8G   1% /dev/shm
efivarfs                         64K   20K   40K  34% /sys/firmware/efi/efivars
tmpfs                           2.4G  1.9M  2.4G   1% /run
none                            1.0M     0  1.0M   0% /run/credentials/systemd-cryptsetup@luks\x2d4ceba41c\x2d2349\x2d42e2\x2daaa7\x2dc40d16426647.service
none                            1.0M     0  1.0M   0% /run/credentials/systemd-journald.service
none                            1.0M     0  1.0M   0% /run/credentials/systemd-resolved.service
tmpfs                           5.8G   12M  5.8G   1% /tmp
/dev/sda2                       9.8G  326M  9.0G   4% /boot
/dev/sda1                       2.0G  7.9M  2.0G   1% /boot/efi
tmpfs                           1.2G  188K  1.2G   1% /run/user/1000

And this is how the disk's space got distributed with the different partitions:

porfirio@taylor:~$ lsblk
NAME                                          MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE  MOUNTPOINTS
sda                                             8:0    0 447.1G  0 disk
├─sda1                                          8:1    0     2G  0 part  /boot/efi
├─sda2                                          8:2    0    10G  0 part  /boot
└─sda3                                          8:3    0 435.1G  0 part
  └─luks-4ceba41c-2349-42e2-aaa7-c40d16426647 252:0    0 435.1G  0 crypt
    └─fedora_taylor-root                      252:1    0 435.1G  0 lvm   /
zram0                                         251:0    0     8G  0 disk  [SWAP]

Enabled Repositories

During the installation I selected the Fedora Workstation Product, which is a set of different Fedora package groups that guarantee that by the end of the installation process you will have the minimal selection of packages that will provide the Workstation experience intended by the Fedora development team.

porfirio@taylor:~$ sudo dnf group list --installed --hidden
[sudo] password for porfirio:
Updating and loading repositories:
Repositories loaded.
ID                        Name                             Installed
base-graphical            base-graphical                         yes
container-management      Container Management                   yes
core                      Core                                   yes
desktop-accessibility     Desktop accessibility                  yes
firefox                   Firefox Web Browser                    yes
fonts                     Fonts                                  yes
gnome-desktop             GNOME                                  yes
guest-desktop-agents      Guest Desktop Agents                   yes
hardware-support          Hardware Support                       yes
libreoffice               LibreOffice                            yes
multimedia                Multimedia                             yes
networkmanager-submodules Common NetworkManager Submodules       yes
printing                  Printing Support                       yes
workstation-product       Fedora Workstation product core        yes
Groups: 14 (14 installed, 0 available)

You can use the command below to get to know more about what packages a package group provides:

dnf group info core

I wanted to make sure which software repositories came enabled by default:

porfirio@taylor:~$ sudo dnf repolist --enabled
repo id                        repo name
fedora                         Fedora 44 - x86_64
fedora-cisco-openh264          Fedora 44 openh264 (From Cisco) - x86_64
updates                        Fedora 44 - x86_64 - Updates

This command lists all the repositories configured but disabled on the system:

porfirio@taylor:~$ sudo dnf repolist --disabled

This command lists all the repositories configured on the system:

porfirio@taylor:~$ dnf repolist --all

List of the installed packages

I wanted to get a copy of all the installed packages just for reference. To get the list of the packages installed and the order in which these packages were installed, I used the following command:

porfirio@taylor:~$ sudo dnf history info 1 > dnfHistoryInfo1_cleanInstall.txt

You can find this file on the link below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/porfiriopaiz/site/refs/heads/master/content/extra/dnfHistoryInfo1_cleanInstall

Finishing Touches

With the base installation complete, the ThinkPad T450 is fully operational with an up-to-date, non-bloated Linux workstation environment built on top of a reliable upstream system architecture.
